title: Far-right links and racist writings of Finns Party ministers in his first weeks (2023)
description: Within weeks of the government taking office, Finns Party ministers faced scrutiny over past statements. Minister of Economic Affairs Vilhelm Junnila survived a no-confidence vote on 28 June 2023 (95–86), with seven of the ten Swedish People's Party MPs voting against him, then announced his resignation on 30 June over jokes referring to Nazism and his links to far-right events; Orpo called this 'the correct and only possible solution'. In July, racist and violent comments posted in 2008 on a blog under the name 'riikka', attributed to Finance Minister and Finns Party leader Riikka Purra, resurfaced; President Sauli Niinistö said the government would be wise to adopt 'zero tolerance' for racism, Orpo said he does not accept racism in any form, and Purra apologised on 11 July but did not resign. Racist private messages from 2016 by Junnila's successor Wille Rydman, published by Helsingin Sanomat, followed; Orpo called them 'inappropriate' but said government cooperation would continue. According to Wikipedia's summary of the coverage, the SPP and Finnish and foreign commentators criticised Orpo's leadership as too weak. The government issued an anti-racism statement in summer 2023 and launched an anti-racism campaign in August 2024, whose commitment experts quoted by Yle questioned.
key_facts: Junnila confidence vote 28 June 2023: 95–86; resignation announced 30 June
Purra's 2008 blog comments surfaced in July 2023; she apologised on 11 July
Rydman's 2016 messages published in July 2023
Anti-racism campaign launched August 2024

title: Union strike wave against the government's labour and social-security reforms (2023–2024)
description: The Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions SAK and other union federations staged a series of political strikes between September 2023 and early April 2024 against the government's labour-market reforms and benefit cuts, including the cap on political strikes, cuts to housing allowances, added waiting days for unemployment benefit and the removal of pay for the first day of sick leave. In December 2023 Orpo called the unions' plans 'unreasonably harsh' given the economic situation and said the reforms were needed to create jobs. The government did not withdraw the measures; the industrial peace law took effect in May 2024.
key_facts: Political strikes from September 2023 to early April 2024 (Yle)
Industrial peace law passed 8 May 2024, in force 18 May 2024

title: Temporary law allowing asylum applications to be refused at the eastern border (2024)
description: Citing Russia's use of migrants for hybrid influence at the eastern border, the government proposed in May 2024 a law allowing border authorities to refuse to accept asylum applications in certain circumstances. The UN refugee agency UNHCR said that pushback procedures put people at risk and that preventing people from seeking international protection violates refugee and human-rights rules. Because it derogates from constitutional provisions it needed a five-sixths majority; Parliament passed it on 12 July 2024 by 167 votes to 31, with the opposition SDP split. Orpo welcomed the vote in the interests of national security and said he hoped the law 'never has to be used'. The law took effect on 22 July 2024 and was extended to the end of 2026; a further government bill on it is pending.
key_facts: UNHCR criticism, 22 May 2024
Passed 12 July 2024 by 167–31 (five-sixths majority required)
Act 482/2024, extended to 31 December 2026 by Act 368/2025

title: Criticism of the distributional effects of spending cuts and tax changes
description: The government's benefit cuts (unemployment benefits, housing allowances, index freezes), the VAT increase to 25.5% in September 2024 and the tax cuts decided in April 2025 drew criticism from unions, opposition parties and some economists. According to a Statistics Finland report cited by Yle, the VAT rise weighs disproportionately on lower-income earners; Yle reported that the 2025 income-tax cuts mostly benefit higher earners, and the chief economist of the Taxpayers' Union told Yle that the purchasing power of the unemployed was 'literally collapsing'. Orpo said the government was taking a risk with the tax cuts but that doing nothing would be riskier, and that the corporate tax cut would bring investment and jobs. After the April 2026 framework talks, which included cuts to social and health-care services, SDP leader Antti Lindtman and Greens leader Sofia Virta called on him to resign; he called this 'very typical opposition rhetoric'. In a Helsingin Sanomat poll published in June 2026, 52% said the government had performed poorly, its worst result of the term.
key_facts: VAT raised to 25.5% on 1 September 2024
April 2025 tax package worth about €2 billion a year
Resignation calls after the April 2026 framework talks
HS poll, June 2026: 52% negative, 21% positive

title: Coalition split over recognising Palestine (2025)
description: After President Alexander Stubb said in late July 2025 that he would approve a government proposal to recognise Palestine, Orpo said on 9 August that the government was not preparing one: he reiterated Kokoomus' support for a two-state solution, which 'logically includes recognising the state of Palestine when the time is right', but said the matter needed further discussion in the government. The Finns Party and the Christian Democrats opposed recognition. According to an Yle source, Orpo had asked Stubb to delay making his position public. On 19 September 2025 the SDP, the Greens and the Left Alliance filed an interpellation over the government's failure to recognise Palestine, saying it left Stubb to attend the UN General Assembly 'empty-handed'. No source consulted for this research reports a recognition proposal by the government.
key_facts: Orpo, 9 August 2025: government not preparing recognition
Finns Party and Christian Democrats opposed
Opposition interpellation, 19 September 2025

title: Apology to East Asian countries over Finns Party MPs' eye-stretching photos (December 2025)
description: After Miss Finland Sarah Dzafce lost her title over a photo of her stretching her eyes with a text referring to a Chinese person, Finns Party MPs Juho Eerola and Kaisa Garedew and MEP Sebastian Tynkkynen posted similar photos, presented as support for her; the images were widely described as racist and offensive to people of Asian descent. On 14 December Orpo called the posts 'childish' and said MPs should set an example of dignified behaviour. On 17 December his apology for the 'offensive social media posts published by individual Members of Parliament' was published on the social-media channels of the Finnish embassies in China, Japan and South Korea, stating that they 'do not reflect Finland's values of equality and non-discrimination'. Eerola apologised; Garedew told Iltalehti she had nothing to apologise for.
key_facts: Orpo's first reaction, 14 December 2025: 'childish'
Apology published by Finnish embassies in China, Japan and South Korea, 17 December 2025

title: Dispute with Finns Party minister Wille Rydman over grants to social and health organisations (2026)
description: On 15 June 2026 Minister of Social Affairs and Health Wille Rydman (Finns) issued new criteria for STEA grants to social and health-care NGOs without agreement in the coalition; Kokoomus and SPP ministers objected, and according to Wikipedia's summary of Finnish reporting there were concerns that cuts targeted sexual and gender minorities. Orpo said Rydman's actions did not follow agreed practice. On 23 June the cabinet voted 10–7 to send the criteria back for preparation, the Finns Party ministers voting against, and the same day Rydman survived a Left Alliance no-confidence motion by 88 votes to 74 after all ten SPP MPs abstained. Orpo said he was 'not pleased with the voting result'; Purra said the SPP had pulled 'the rug out from under the prime minister's feet'. On 13 August the government unanimously adopted a decree on the grant criteria that Orpo had called for; Rydman said his own criteria were not legally or politically binding, and SPP leader Anders Adlercreutz said the decree removed their 'discriminatory features'. The €84 million cut to STEA grants itself had been agreed unanimously.
key_facts: Cabinet vote of 23 June 2026: 10–7
Rydman confidence vote: 88–74, ten SPP abstentions
Decree adopted unanimously on 13 August 2026

title: Garden Helsinki arena subsidy and confidence vote (2025–2026)
description: In its spring 2025 mid-term budget framework the government earmarked a conditional €35 million state subsidy for Garden Helsinki, a long-planned multi-purpose arena in Helsinki's Töölö district, although the Finance Ministry had earlier taken a critical view of support (Yle). Kokoomus brought the matter to the government, the project was lobbied by Kokoomus figure Jan Vapaavuori, and construction company SRV, whose main owner Ilpo Kokkila has donated to Kokoomus and to Orpo's campaigns, was involved. Opposition parties criticised the secrecy of the preparation and alleged preferential treatment; the National Audit Office examined whether the project company should have registered its lobbying in the transparency register. On 20 July 2026 Orpo announced that the governing parties had withdrawn their political support, citing a scaled-back and delayed project, 'clear shortcomings in the lobbying process' and a changed competitive situation. Speaker Jussi Halla-aho recalled Parliament from its summer recess; after a government statement and a nine-hour debate, Parliament expressed confidence in Orpo and in the government on 21 July 2026, each time by 101 votes to 90. Orpo denied that election donations had played any role.
key_facts: Conditional €35 million subsidy decided in spring 2025
Support withdrawn 20 July 2026
Confidence votes 21 July 2026: 101–90

title: Chancellor of Justice inquiry into possible disqualification (Valmet Automotive and Garden Helsinki)
description: Complaints were filed with the Chancellor of Justice (oikeuskansleri), who oversees the legality of the government's actions, about whether Orpo should have recused himself from two decisions: the state's rescue of car manufacturer Valmet Automotive in Uusikaupunki in October 2025, worth about €120 million, after which the state owns about 80% of the company and Pontos Oy, an investment company founded by Ilpo Kokkila, about 20%; and the Garden Helsinki subsidy, in which Kokkila's company SRV was involved. According to Yle, citing Iltalehti, Kokkila has given Kokoomus more than €120,000 over about fifteen years, and his investment companies gave Orpo €3,000 (Afortus, 2025 municipal election) and €1,000 (Pontos, 2021 municipal election). In July 2026 Chancellor Janne Salminen asked Orpo to answer a list of questions by the end of August. In his reply, reported on 31 August 2026, Orpo stated that he was not disqualified 'on any grounds', that neither he nor anyone close to him had gained or could expect any benefit, and that Kokkila's donations had not been out of the ordinary; he had earlier said on Yle's A-studio that he did not take part in preparing the Valmet decision and saw no reason to recuse himself because the effect was relatively small. As of October 2026 no decision by the Chancellor had been reported. The inquiry is legality oversight of a minister, not a criminal or court proceeding.
key_facts: Valmet Automotive rescue, October 2025: about €120 million of state capital
Kokkila-linked companies' donations to Orpo: €1,000 (2021) and €3,000 (2025), per Yle/Iltalehti
Orpo's reply to the Chancellor, 31 August 2026: denies disqualification
No decision reported as of October 2026

title: Financing of his 2016 party leadership campaign
description: Yle reported in September 2016 that Orpo's campaign for the Kokoomus chairmanship, which cost €46,000 against €43,000 of income, was run through the account of the party's Varsinais-Suomi district, whose board had decided to back him: the district's executive director handled the finances on working time paid by the party, the district covered the €3,000 loss and a district-linked foundation gave €5,000. Rival candidates Alexander Stubb and Elina Lepomäki told Yle they had received no financial support from party organisations, and according to Yle the arrangement caused irritation within the party. The district director said it followed established party practice and that every individual contribution was under €1,500; Yle named businessmen including Ilpo Kokkila among the campaign's supporters. No breach of rules was alleged in the reporting.
key_facts: Campaign costs €46,000; income €43,000 (Yle)
District organisation covered a €3,000 loss
